note: Proposes a benchmark lifecycle covering design, validation, monitoring and retirement, an audit ready framing.
title: Beyond the Leaderboard: A Survey of the Science of Evaluation, Benchmarking, and Methodologies for Large Language Models

reading.body:
Popular benchmarks for large language models do not measure what developers and buyers believe they measure, creating systematic misprediction of real-world performance.

The gap between leaderboard scores and actual capability has become a structural problem in AI evaluation. Models that rank highly on standard tests frequently fail in deployment by making errors or producing harmful outputs that the benchmarks never surface. This disconnect arises because evaluation instruments remain static while model behavior evolves, enabling data contamination and gaming of specific metrics. The problem is not merely methodological. It is economic. Organizations making deployment decisions based on published scores face compounded risk: they may select inferior systems, overpay for marginal improvements, or discover after investment that capabilities do not match expectations.

The paper proposes treating evaluation itself as a lifecycle rather than a leaderboard. The framework moves through design of measurement instruments, validation that they measure genuine capability, monitoring performance in use, and retirement when instruments become obsolete or compromised. This systematization matters because it treats benchmarks as tools requiring maintenance rather than permanent facts. Five evaluation approaches emerge from the survey: static benchmarks, dynamic adaptive testing, interactive agentic evaluation, human-in-the-loop methods, and model-based evaluation. Each addresses different aspects of capability but none alone captures what deployed systems must actually do.

The data does not specify which benchmarks failed most severely, which companies suffered material losses from misprediction, or how much compute and infrastructure cost was wasted on models selected through unreliable metrics. It does not measure the performance of the proposed lifecycle framework in practice or compare its cost to current evaluation approaches. These gaps mean the paper identifies a real problem in how AI capability is assessed but cannot quantify its economic impact on the compute and power infrastructure decisions that follow from benchmark-driven model selection.

explain_beginner: This paper identifies a major problem in AI: popular test scores for large language models do not actually measure what we think they measure. Although these AI systems score well on standard tests, they often fail in real situations by making mistakes or producing harmful content. The researchers argue we need better evaluation methods that assess genuine capabilities rather than pursuing high scores on leaderboards. They propose a structured lifecycle for creating, checking, and retiring evaluation tools to make progress measurement more trustworthy.
explain_business: Organizations deploying large language models face a critical risk: public benchmark scores do not predict real-world performance. This paper demonstrates why relying solely on leaderboard rankings to select models is unreliable and why purchased or built systems may underperform expectations. The proposed Benchmark Lifecycle framework provides a structured methodology for enterprises to properly evaluate AI systems before deployment, reducing failure risk. This guidance helps organizations establish evaluation as a scientific process rather than a competitive metric, ensuring confident decision-making for AI investments.
explain_practitioner: The survey examines the disconnect between benchmark performance and practical LLM capabilities, attributing it to static evaluation paradigms. The authors present a taxonomy covering five evaluation approaches: static benchmarks, dynamic adaptive evaluation, interactive agentic evaluation, human-in-the-loop methods, and model-based evaluation. They analyze key pathologies including data contamination and leaderboard gaming. The central contribution is the Benchmark Lifecycle framework, which systematizes evaluation instrument development through design, validation, deployment monitoring, and retirement phases to enable rigorous measurement aligned with actual model behavior.
